name: Font Family Role Selection
use_when: A video needs a font system for titles, captions, labels, lower thirds, or hook text.
The agent must match typography to project tone, industry, or client reference.
A design feels random because fonts are being chosen without roles.
A documentary or explainer needs editorial, archival, source-label, or cinematic title fonts without copying a publisher identity.
A social edit needs clean modern sans text, Apple-inspired presentation text, or controlled font-shift emphasis.
avoid_when: A client brand guide already defines approved fonts and hierarchy.
The chosen expressive font is not readable at final size.
The edit needs plain accessibility captions more than a stylized type system.

timeline_pattern.pattern: project_tone -> industry_or_reference -> choose_family_role -> choose_primary_and_support_fonts -> apply_to_text_roles -> delivery_size_qc

family_roles.serif: Use for editorial, history, archival, or documentary gravity when it remains readable.
family_roles.sans_serif: Use for clean modern technology, education, product, and utility text.
family_roles.script: Use sparingly for handwritten, personal, artistic, or playful accents.
family_roles.display: Use for bold headlines, poster energy, YouTube-style titles, or high-impact words.

documentary_examples.archival_display: Special Elite or another typewriter/archival-feeling font can work for short historic labels when readable.
documentary_examples.editorial_serif: Times New Roman or another strong serif can work for historical/documentary gravity.
documentary_examples.clean_sans: A clean sans such as Tarful Sans Pro or an equivalent can support labels and modern documentary utility text.
documentary_examples.condensed_headline: A condensed bold sans such as Helvetica Black Condensed or an equivalent can work for strong title words.

timeline_pattern.pairing_rule: Pair one expressive family with one neutral support family; avoid making two loud fonts compete.
timeline_pattern.consistency_rule: Keep the same family roles across the edit unless a story shift deliberately changes the type language.

motion.rule: Font family choice comes before motion; do not animate a type style that already fails tone or readability.

keyframe_values.family_change: Use a font-family shift only on a clear section, tone, character, or perspective change.
keyframe_values.social_font_shift: A font-shift loop should be brief and tied to a word or phrase that benefits from style contrast; return to the base font before the next reading task.
keyframe_values.capcut_social_fonts: Clean bold sans fonts such as Fig Tree Bold work for premium perspective or highlight text; stylized display fonts such as Droid-style title faces belong only on short reveal phrases.
keyframe_values.display_hold: Give display or script text slightly more hold time than plain sans text.
keyframe_values.documentary_title_animation: In CapCut documentary title moments, animation duration around 1.5-2 seconds can feel more professional than very fast template motion when the word remains readable.
keyframe_values.cinematic_open_animation: A cinematic open-style text animation can start around 1.3 seconds, then tune by word length and narration pace.

sound.rule: No direct sound rule; use SFX only if the type entrance is an intentional beat.

captions.rule: Use readable serif or sans fonts for continuous captions; reserve script/display fonts for isolated emphasis words or title moments.

color.rule: Font family and color should support the same tone; do not pair a serious family choice with random accent colors.

implementation.ffmpeg: Use explicit fontfile paths for drawtext and keep a style map for title, caption, label, and emphasis roles.
implementation.remotion: Store familyRole, primaryFont, supportFont, expressiveFont, and textRole tokens in the project style object.
implementation.blender: Use text objects with assigned materials by role; preview camera framing before locking font choice.
implementation.capcut_equivalent: Choose text styles by role, not by template novelty; keep one primary font lane and one accent lane. Clean sans fonts such as Inter Semi Bold, Arial Bold, or Fig Tree Bold can support modern social text when spacing and contrast are checked. Use stylized display fonts only for short title/reveal moments. For font-shift loops, blade only the phrase that needs the shift and deselect the loop when returning to the base font. For documentary titles, test restrained animations around 1.5-2 seconds and verify the text settles before it must be read.
implementation.premiere_equivalent: Create Essential Graphics styles or Track Styles for each role, then apply them consistently across titles, captions, labels, and hooks.

common_mistakes: Using a font because it looks premium while it mismatches the subject.
Using script or display fonts for long captions.
Changing fonts every scene without a story, brand, or reference reason.
Letting a font-shift loop keep changing after the viewer needs a stable word to read.
Pairing two expressive fonts so neither one has hierarchy.
Copying the exact font mix of a publisher reference instead of adapting the role system to the project.
qc: Does the font family match the project tone and industry reference?
Is there one primary font lane and one support/accent lane?
Are continuous captions still readable at phone size?
Do expressive fonts appear only where their readability cost is justified?
Do documentary title animations settle before the viewer needs to read the word or source label?
